extracted.intended_audience: architects, artists, handicraftsmen, and critics interested in ethical/aesthetic principles of architectural practice
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and moral principles governing honesty, representation, materials, and structural truth in architecture and allied arts (painting, decoration). Focuses on avoiding deceptive expedients and preserving dignity of the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lamp of Truth / general moral duty to truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth forgives no insult, and endures no stain; artists and handicraftsmen should practise truthfulness as habit rather than occasional heroism—'Do not let us lie at all.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truth is a habit to be formed by constant practice; speaking and acting truth with constancy and precision is nearly as difficult and meritorious as speaking it under intimidation. The principle of truth should guide artists' acts and pleasures, ennobling handicrafts by 'the spurs of chivalry.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination must confess its ideality
rubrics_metrics.description: The imagination is noble so long as it 'confesses its own ideality'; when it ceases to confess this it becomes insanity. The difference between noble imagination and deception lies in the confession that the object is not actually present or real.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voluntary summoning of absent or impossible conceptions is legitimate provided the artist/observer knows they are not actual. Deceptive imagination (presenting false belief of reality) is morally and artistically wrong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Painting as representation, not assertion of existence
rubrics_metrics.description: Painting is, on the contrary, 'a statement of certain facts, in the clearest possible way'—it communicates shape and colour without asserting physical existence. The lie consists only in an assertion of existence or false statements of forms and colours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A communicated act of imagination is not a lie if there is no assertion or belief in its actual existence. Good painting 'makes [its ground] more precious' but does not claim to be the material it is painted upon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural Deceits — threefold taxonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Architectural Deceits are broadly to be considered under three heads: (1) the suggestion of a mode of structure or support other than the true one; (2) the painting of surfaces to represent some other material than that of which they actually consist; (3) the use of cast or machine-made ornaments of any kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid these false expedients; architecture will be noble exactly in the degree in which all these false expedients are avoided. Some degrees, by frequent usage or other causes, may have lost the nature of deceit and be admissible, but the broad rule is against deceptive devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of structural deceit (false suggestion of support)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not suggest a mode of structure or support other than the true one (e.g., making an intermediate vault of wood and whitewashing it to look like stone is direct deceit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The architect is not bound to exhibit structure nor is concealment always blameworthy: concealment is permissible where weight/support would be unknown to a spectator. But once the conditions of weight/support are comprehended, 'truth and feeling require that the conditions of support should be also comprehended.' Affectedly inadequate supports and 'suspensions in air' are especially condemned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid deceptive assumptions of structure (decorative members with no duty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not introduce members which profess to have a structural duty but have none (e.g., buttresses, pinnacles or flying buttresses used decoratively where they perform no structural function).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decorative appropriation of structural forms that perform no work is blameable—examples include pinnacles used merely as ornament or pierced buttresses with no resisting thrust. Such mockeries are 'sickly phantoms and mockeries of things that were.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface deceits: do not paint surfaces to represent different materials
rubrics_metrics.description: The painting of surfaces to induce the supposition of some form or material which does not actually exist (e.g., painting wood to look like marble, painting ornaments in deceptive relief) is base and inadmissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Painting confessedly as painting is legitimate; the evil lies in definite attempted deception. Contextual distinctions matter: fresco or painted decoration clearly acknowledged as such (Sistine Chapel, Campo Santo, Parma cupola) are acceptable; shop-front marbling, faux-marble church decoration, and painted imitations that deceive or cast suspicion on true materials are to be condemned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible painted illusion only when confessed or unmistakably painting
rubrics_metrics.description: Painted architecture or figurative illusion is lawful when the work is clearly known to be painting (the artist 'stops short' of gross deception) or when the subject precludes possibility of deception (e.g., heavenly visions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the Sistine Chapel's painted architecture is acceptable because it is integrated with figures and known to be painting; Correggio's cupola, though deceptively powerful, is allowed because the subject precludes real belief. In gardens, villas, and places of idleness some toy-like illusions may be innocent if regarded as mere play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of false representation of material in high architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: All imitations of material (e.g., marbling, mock granite, false marble) in architecture of a higher rank are 'utterly base and inadmissible.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such imitations degrade honesty of whole building and may cast suspicion on true materials elsewhere (example: imitation granite landing at British Museum). The practice wastes resources and is contemptible, especially in places of worship where simplicity and purity are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of cast or machine-made ornaments discouraged
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of cast or machine-made ornaments of any kind is listed as one of the primary architectural deceits and is to be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Machine-made decorative substitutes remove honesty and individuality from architecture; they are aligned with other deceptive expedients and indicate a debasement of the arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule for metals: 'metals may be used as a cement but not as a support'
rubrics_metrics.description: Metals (iron) may enter construction as cement-like elements (rivets, bands) but must not be used as primary supports bearing crushing weight or replacing buttresses or stone supports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If metal takes the place of stone as a support, or bears superincumbent weight, the building 'ceases, so far as such applications of metal extend, to be true architecture.' Excessive or extravagant metal use derogates from dignity and honesty. Exceptions allowed where metal performs a cementing function or in minor reinforcing roles (e.g., Brunelleschi's iron chain) provided the metal could in principle be superseded by good masonry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer stone joinery and craftsmanship before resorting to metal
rubrics_metrics.description: Before using metal to assist mortar, fit and dovetail stones and apply good masonry; reliance on iron should not permit slovenly workmanship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where artifice is necessary to help the mortar, such stone-fitting should come before the use of metal. Metal may be used for delicacy and security in some parts, but only after exhausting honest stonework solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty valued above apparent grandeur or invention
rubrics_metrics.description: It is better to have an honest architecture (even if meagre or utilitarian) than a deceitful one; the meagreness of poverty may be pardoned and utility respected, but deception merits scorn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first practical step toward greatness is to eliminate petty dishonesties. Architects may not be able to command invention, but they can command honesty. Voluntary restraints and submission to material/structural limits demonstrate greatness and wisdom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and purity required in sacred architecture and church furniture
rubrics_metrics.description: Church furniture and decoration should be simple and unaffected, 'not fictitious nor tawdry'; false marbles, painted iron, and tawdry upholstery are especially reprehensible in houses of worship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if resources are limited, choose solid stone and wood, whitewash if necessary; false ornament in sacred contexts is offensive and may obstruct devotional repose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual exceptions and degrees of admissibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Some deceptive expedients (e.g., gilding, certain decorative devices) may be admissible where their meaning is universally understood or they have 'lost the nature of deceit' by common usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge exceptions by whether the device is understood as ornament (gilding in architecture is not deceit because not taken for gold) and by the dignity of the artist: greater leniency may be given to great painters and designers who will not 'paint badly enough to deceive.'
